title: Independence and autonomy
description: Independence is having increasing opportunities to do things for yourself. Autonomy includes making choices and having those choices respected. A child can participate meaningfully while still using communication tools, adaptations or another person’s support.
example: Choose one routine that matters to your child: selecting clothes, opening a lunchbox or asking for a break. Describe what they already do and the help that makes the next step possible.
question: Which part could my child choose or do themselves, and how will we recognise useful progress?

title: Planning and organisation
description: Planning means working out the steps in an activity. Organisation means keeping the materials and information needed for those steps accessible. These abilities show up in familiar routines long before a child can explain a plan in words.
example: Packing a school bag brings several steps together: choose the items, find them, put them in the bag and check what is missing. Pictures or a short checklist can make the sequence visible.
question: Is the difficulty knowing the next step, finding an item, remembering the sequence or handling the object?

title: Play and imagination
description: Play offers many ways to explore, connect and express an idea. Imaginative play can include pretending, telling a story or giving a familiar object a new role. Different children enjoy different forms of play.
example: Follow your child’s interest in a toy animal or vehicle. A shared game might begin with one action, such as feeding the animal or parking the car, and grow when the child is interested.
question: What does my child already enjoy, and how can we join that play without taking it over?

title: Restricted interests and repetitive behaviours
description: Repeated movements, routines and strong interests can be part of an autistic person’s experience. Understanding what an activity means to the child matters: enjoyment, predictability, communication, comfort or another need. Harmless differences do not automatically need to be stopped.
example: Notice when a routine becomes difficult to change and what helps the child feel prepared. Bring a concrete example from home or school to the team, including what happened before and afterwards.
question: Is there distress, a safety concern or a barrier to participation, and what support would address that particular need?

title: Miller Function and Participation Scales
description: The Miller Function and Participation Scales, often called M-FUN, is an assessment tool concerned with children’s motor performance and participation. A professional chooses and interprets an assessment in the context of the child and the question being asked.
example: Bring examples of everyday tasks, such as drawing, managing classroom materials or joining physical play. Ask how any assessment findings relate to those activities.
question: Why is this tool suitable for my child, what are its limits and how will the findings shape practical goals?

title: NEPSY-II assessment
description: NEPSY-II is a developmental neuropsychological assessment battery. Its tasks can contribute to a professional understanding of a child’s functioning. Selecting tasks and interpreting results requires the appropriate training and a clear assessment question.
example: A parent or teacher can describe specific situations that need explanation: following instructions, remembering a sequence or managing a learning activity. Those observations help frame the professional discussion.
question: Who would administer and interpret the assessment, and what useful decisions would its findings inform?

title: Kids LED study desk lamp
description: A desk lamp changes the lighting around a reading, drawing or table activity. It is an environmental item; its presence alone does not establish a developmental or therapeutic benefit.
example: Look at the task area with your child. Check whether the page is easy to see, whether glare is distracting and whether the lamp leaves enough working space.
question: Would changing the lighting or position make this particular activity more comfortable?

title: Party horn noisemakers
description: A party horn is a sound-making celebration item. Noise, detachable parts and items used near the mouth make the exact product and the child’s preferences important. It should not be presented as a treatment for speech delay.
example: For a turn-taking sound game, ask the therapist to select an age-appropriate sound toy the child enjoys. Agree on a clear way for the child to say stop or choose a quieter activity.

title: Gift wrapping paper sheets
description: Wrapping paper can be a craft material for folding, choosing patterns and preparing a gift. An everyday craft has more meaning when the child understands the purpose and has a real choice in it.

description: A cushion sold with a belt is not evidence that it is an approved child car restraint. For travel, choose a suitable child restraint and follow both its manufacturer’s instructions and the vehicle guidance.

title: Reading overlay strips
description: A reading overlay strip is a coloured or clear guide placed over text. A child may have an individual preference about how a page looks, but a preference does not establish treatment of dyslexia or replace a reading assessment.
example: Ask the teacher to identify the actual reading difficulty and compare how the child manages the same task with their usual support. Record comfort separately from reading accuracy or comprehension.

title: Kids drum set musical toy

title: Magnetic pen drawing board

title: Cross trainer equipment

title: Modular storage containers

title: Balance and hopping
description: Balance helps a person maintain or change position. Hopping involves moving from and landing on one foot. These skills matter in different ways for play and everyday movement, with development varying between children.
example: Describe a real activity the child wants to join, such as a playground game. A professional can help identify the movement demands and suitable support.

title: Communication and pre-literacy
description: Pre-literacy includes the experiences that support later reading and writing: enjoying books, noticing sounds and symbols, sharing meaning and making marks. Communication can include speech, gesture and other tools.

description: Receptive communication concerns understanding messages. Expressive communication concerns sharing a message with someone else. A child may use speech, gestures, pictures or a communication device, and their abilities can differ across situations.

title: Sorting and categorisation
description: Sorting means putting things into groups using a feature or rule. Categorisation involves understanding which things belong together. Everyday objects can make the purpose of a group easier to understand.
example: Sort familiar items by what they are used for, or match a small set by one visible feature. Ask the child to show their idea rather than insisting on only one possible grouping.
